profile.title_role: Ph.D. Researcher in Materials Science & Engineering
profile.bio: As a Doctoral Researcher at Sungkyunkwan University pursuing a Doctor of Science degree, I focus on advancing the field through innovative simulations and leveraging strong analytical skills. My academic foundation includes a Master’s Degree in Physics from Hanoi University of Science and Technology (2024). I collaborate on research initiatives aimed at addressing critical energy challenges, utilizing simulation tools to analyze complex systems. My work reflects a commitment to driving impactful solutions in semiconductor technologies while contributing to academic and scientific advancements.

papers.title: Hole-doping induced ferromagnetism in 2D materials
papers.authors: Ruishen Meng, Lino da Costa Pereira, Jean-Pierre Locquet, Valeri Afanas’ev, Geoffrey Pourtois
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic materials are considered as promising candidates for the future generations of spintronic devices. Yet, 2D materials with intrinsic ferromagnetism are scarce. Hereby, high-throughput first-principles simulations are performed to screen 2D materials that present a non-magnetic to a ferromagnetic transition upon hole doping. A global evolutionary search is subsequently performed to identify alternative possible atomic structures of the eligible candidates, and 122 materials exhibiting a hole-doping induced ferromagnetism are identified. Their energetic and dynamic stability, as well as magnetic properties under hole doping are investigated systematically. Half of these 2D materials are metal halides, followed by chalcogenides, oxides, and nitrides, some of them having predicted Curie temperatures above 300 K. The exchange interactions responsible for the ferromagnetic order are also discussed. This work not only provides theoretical insights into hole-doped 2D ferromagnetic materials, but also enriches the family of 2D magnetic materials for possible spintronic applications.

papers.title: Antisite defect qubits in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides
papers.authors: Jeng-Yuan Tsai, Jinbo Pan, Hsin Lin, Arun Bansil, Qimin Yan
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Being atomically thin and amenable to external controls, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a new paradigm for the realization of patterned qubit fabrication and operation at room temperature for quantum information sciences applications. Here we show that the antisite defect in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can provide a controllable solid-state spin qubit system. Using high-throughput atomistic simulations, we identify several neutral antisite defects in TMDs that lie deep in the bulk band gap and host a paramagnetic triplet ground state. Our in-depth analysis reveals the presence of optical transitions and triplet-singlet intersystem crossing processes for fingerprinting these defect qubits. As an illustrative example, we discuss the initialization and readout principles of an antisite qubit in WS
                    2
                    , which is expected to be stable against interlayer interactions in a multilayer structure for qubit isolation and protection in future qubit-based devices. Our study opens a new pathway for creating scalable, room-temperature spin qubits in 2D TMDs.
papers.notes: Good reference for antisite defects in TMDs.

papers.title: Universal hydrogen-free synthesis and elemental doping of two-dimensional transition metal selenides
papers.authors: Ping Man, Lok Wing Wong, Ka Ho Leung, Zhiqiang Guan, Tianren Chen, Honglin Chen et al.
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal selenides (TMSs) feature notable bandgap flexibility, versatile doping characteristics, and practical manufacturability, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation electronics. However, their synthesis remains a critical bottleneck, as conventional chemical vapor deposition (CVD) routes require H2 assistance for selenization, raising safety, cost, and quality concerns and constraining elemental doping. Here we show a universal, H2-free CVD method that overcomes these limitations. Our approach produces a broad spectrum of 2D TMSs, including monolayer binaries, bilayer polytypes, alloys, and heterostructures, and is compatible with diverse substrates. Incorporating common metals (Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Cu) into the precursor enhances growth kinetics and enables precise doping. Al-doped WSe2 exhibits markedly lower resistance, with centimeter-scale films attaining a hole mobility of 28.36 cm2 V−1 s−1 and an on/off ratio of 3.56×106, comparable to exfoliated and H2-assisted monolayers. This work establishes a safe, scalable, and tunable synthesis strategy for high-performance 2D electronics. 2D transition metal selenides (TMSs) exhibit interesting (opto-)electronic properties, but their bottom-up synthesis usually requires H2 gas, leading to safety concerns and cost implications. Here, the authors report a universal H2-free chemical vapour deposition method to grow large-scale metal-doped 2D TMSs on various substrates.

papers.title: What Is the Role of a Magnetic Mo Antisite Defect on Carrier Relaxation and Spin Dynamics in 2-D MoS<sub>2</sub>?
papers.authors: Chengan Lei, Zhao Qian, Yandong Ma, Rajeev Ahuja
papers.abstract: Antisite defects significantly influence the dynamic properties of monolayer MoS 2, yet the carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in spin-polarized Mo antisite-defective MoS 2 remain unclear. Understanding these processes is crucial for advancing optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices. Here, we employ first-principles calculations and ab initio nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with spin–orbit coupling (SOC) to explore carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with a Mo antisite defect. This defect alters the material’s magnetic properties, leading to distinct relaxation behaviors: electron relaxation is slower than hole relaxation, and charge carriers in different spin channels exhibit varied dynamics. These differences arise from variations in electron–phonon coupling, SOC strength, and phonon mode activation. Our findings provide key insights into charge and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with magnetic defects and suggest strategies to enhance the performance of next-generation optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices.

news_articles.title: Hybrid Bonding Basics: What Is Hybrid Bonding?
news_articles.content_html:
Hybrid bonding is the key to paving an innovative future in advanced packaging. Hybrid bonding provides a solution that enables higher bandwidth and increased power and signal integrity. As the industry is looking to enhance the performance of final devices through scaling system-level interconnections, hybrid bonding provides the most promising solution with the ability to integrate several dies with small interconnection pitches below 10 µm. Understanding the basics of hybrid bonding requires asking three fundamental questions: What is hybrid bonding, why use hybrid bonding, and which material is best suited for your application?

What is hybrid bonding?

Understanding hybrid bonding requires a brief history of the advanced packaging industry. When the electronics packaging industry evolved to three-dimensional packaging, microbumps provided vertical interconnects between chips by using small copper bumps on dies as one form of wafer-level packaging. Bumps range in size, from 40-µm pitch to eventually being scaled down to 20-µm or 10-µm pitches. However, this is where the issue arises; scaling down past 10µm becomes very challenging and engineers are turning to a new solution to continue to scale size smaller. Hybrid bonding provides a solution for 10 µm pitches and below by completely avoiding the use of bumps, and instead connects dies in packages using small copper-to-copper connections. It provides superior interconnect density, enabling 3D-like packages and advanced memory cubes.

Hybrid bonding is a permanent bond that combines a dielectric bond (SiOx) with embedded metal (Cu) to form interconnections. It’s become known industry-wide as direct bond interconnect (DBI). Hybrid bonding extends fusion bonding with embedded metal pads in the bond interface, which allows face-to-face connection of the wafers.

Why use hybrid bonding?

Hybrid bonding vertically connects die-to-wafer (D2W) or wafer-to-wafer (W2W) via closely spaced copper pads. While W2W hybrid bonding has been in production for several years in image sensing, there is a strong industry push to expedite the development of D2W hybrid bonding. This development will further enable heterogeneous integration, which provides a powerful and flexible means to directly connect die of different functions, sizes, and design rules.

Hybrid bonding offers many advantages over other bonding techniques, including:

  • Allows advanced 3D device stacking
  • Highest I/O
  • Enables sub-10-µm bonding pitch
  • Higher memory density
  • Expanded bandwidth
  • Increased power
  • Improved speed efficiency
  • Eliminates the need for bumps, improving performance with no power and signal penalties

Image Credit: Imed Jani. Test and characterization of 3D high-density interconnects. Micro and Nanotechnologies/Microelectronics. Université Grenoble Alpes, 2019. English. NNT : 2019GREAT094 . tel- 02634259

Inorganic vs polymeric dielectric materials for hybrid bonding

The main differences between SiOx/metal hybrid bonding and polymer/metal hybrid bonding are illustrated in the chart below.

Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) is one of the key processes in wafer-level packaging. CMP is a process that removes materials by a combination of chemical and mechanical actions to achieve highly smooth and planar material surfaces. Achieving a planar surface through a CMP process is expensive, which is one of the shortcomings of using SiOx as the dielectric material. SiOx requires a planar surface roughness (Ra) of less than 1 nm through CMP. Not achieving a planar surface can be detrimental, as particles or Cu dishing will cause voids in bond lines. Additionally, SiOx has no reflow during bond which can cause air gaps around the metal.

Below is a simplified process to show how a permanent bonding adhesive can be used in hybrid bonding. In case A, a dielectric polymer is applied over Cu pillars and then planarized before bonding. In case B, the polymer is patterned and the Cu pillar is formed via a dual damascene approach before bonding. The functionality of a photopatternable dielectric material makes this flow possible.

Hybrid bonding is an innovative technology being developed for next-generation packaged devices. The latest photosensitive permanent bonding material will be an enabler and complement Brewer Science’s permanent bonding expertise. This overview discusses the basics of hybrid bonding for a fundamental understanding; however if you are looking to learn more about hybrid bonding specific to your application please schedule a call with an expert or download the white paper, which provides thorough research on the differences between a new polymeric material in comparison to using silicon oxide as the dielectric. The white paper presents material characterization, process optimization, reliability, and preliminary polymer/polymer hybrid bonding results.

news_articles.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
news_articles.keywords: International Business, Singapore, Nvidia, Semiconductors, Artificial intelligence, China, China-US relations, Asia
news_articles.abstract: A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
news_articles.content_html:
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.

For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.

With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.

But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

Megaspeed is a case in point.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.

They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.

The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.

But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.

Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.

In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.

Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.

Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.

Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.

Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.

On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".

China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.

How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.

But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.

Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.

BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.

In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.

Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.

Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.

All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".

But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.

With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.

"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".

"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

news_articles.title: Personal Rehabilitation: Means for a Healthy Economy?
news_articles.subtitle: Personal Rehabilitation: Means for a Healthy Economy?
news_articles.abstract: On July 1st, the Seoul Bankruptcy Court (SLBC) began to apply a new rule: to prepare a support plan for debtors who have failed to invest in stocks or cryptocurrency. However, there have been opinions that by applying this rule, the SLBC will be helping those who went into debt in order to invest. Therefore, the Sungkyun Times (SKT) will examine the definition of personal rehabilitation and the discussion surrounding the SLBC regulation.
news_articles.content_html:
What is Personal Rehabilitation?

Meaning of Personal Rehabilitation

“Personal rehabilitation” is a system in which an individual’s debt is reduced or eliminated if the court decides that the debtor might face bankruptcy. To register for personal rehabilitation, the debtor should meet the following qualifications. First, the amount of debt must be larger than the individual’s total property. Furthermore, the debtor should be an employee who receives a regular salary or should be selfemployed. Lastly, the debtor should be on the verge of being unable to repay their debts. After the qualified debtor submits the required documents, including a repayment plan and a list of their properties, the repayment plan is approved. Then, the debtor should repay the debt within three years unless there are special reasons. After the debtor repays the fixed amount of debt, the debt apart from the repayment plan is exempted. On the other hand, there is also a system called the “personal bankruptcy system,” but this system divides the debtor’s property equally among the creditors. In principle, the debtor must pay back a larger amount through personal rehabilitation than through the personal bankruptcy system. In other words, those who apply for personal rehabilitation must repay a larger amount than their property: thus, the “rule of assuring liquidating value.” For example, if an individual’s debt is 800 million won, and his property’s value is 200 million won, the debtor must repay at the least 200 million won.

New Rule by the SLBC

Starting from July 1st, the SLBC passed a new rule indicating that investment losses in stocks or cryptocurrency are not included in the liquidation value when fixing the amount of debt for personal rehabilitation. For instance, if a debtor lent 1 billion won and invested it all in cryptocurrency but lost 800 million due to a decrease in value, the court settles tender to be only 200 million won. Recently, individuals, especially those in their 20s and 30s, who have failed to invest in stocks or cryptocurrency have increased. Hence, the SLBC legislated the new rule to lessen the trend of rising debt. In fact, this year, the market capitalization of the top five virtual asset exchanges became 22 trillion won. This is nearly 31 trillion won less compared to last year. Such data shows that many investors have suffered from losses. Experts claim that the 2030 generation tends to invest their entire property. Furthermore, as they frequently access social media, they quickly feel relative deprivation. Accordingly, the SLBC expects the new rule to help those in the 2030 generation suffering from investment failure in stocks and cryptocurrency to restore their economic activities.

Seoul Bankruptcy Court (SLBC) (brunch.co.kr)

Support for Social Return versus Excessive Incentive to Investment?

Providing a Chance to Return

1. Focusing on Personal Rehabilitation

Personal rehabilitation aims to guarantee economic revival by protecting the debtor’s fundamental property and the creditor’s rights. The rule protects the debtor’s rights by aiding the debtor to repay a measure of debt based on one’s salary or personal business, rather than bankruptcy, which confiscates the debtor’s property. Furthermore, the court also holds creditors as “investment losers” who failed to invest, as they lent money to debtors with no ability to repay. Rather than undergoing bankruptcy, in which debtors repay a lesser amount, personal rehabilitation benefits both the debtors and creditors, as debtors must repay the creditors steadily through their stable gains. Thus, for debtors to apply for personal rehabilitation, the rule of assuring liquidating value is vital. In the traditional rule, which includes losses from investment in the liquidating value, debtors must repay an even higher amount of debt even though they have already lost money. If the court determines that the debtor’s property is larger than the investment losses, the debtor cannot apply for personal rehabilitation and must choose bankruptcy – therefore, the creditor also receives a smaller amount of repayment. However, the new rule allows the court to determine the liquidating value while considering the debtor’s property. Thus, debtors who could not apply for personal rehabilitation due to a high amount of loss are now eligible to apply. By expanding cases of personal rehabilitation, the rights of both debtors and creditors will be guaranteed.

A Life-Threatening Debt (oracleag.com)

2. Securing Equity with Other Types of Assets

The new rule helps stock and cryptocurrency procure the same position as other assets, such as real estate. Before the new rule was implemented, the reason for including losses on investing in stocks or cryptocurrency in the tender was to reduce the debtor’s moral hazard and consider the volatility of the assets. However, in the case of real estate plans, the court settles the tender when approving the repayment plan, regardless of whether the asset may have decreased compared to the purchased price. According to Yonhap News, a high court judge who worked in the bankruptcy department of the district court explained that “the tender should be settled based on the price of the asset at the point of procuring the plan.” Also, although the rule may seem “new” as it was recently applied, this is only because cryptocurrency is a comparatively modern type of asset, not because the rule itself is new. According to the traditional rule, the investment principal of stock or cryptocurrency was included in the bond disallowed for exemption, but it is hard to find a reliable precedent case that actually regards stocks and cryptocurrency. Furthermore, there is a claim that the nation already admits exchanges through verified bank accounts, and that stock and cryptocurrency are new types of assets. Thus, the previous rule of exempting loss from the tender should also be applied to stocks and cryptocurrency, as they are simply
comparatively new types of assets.

Who Encouraged Debt-Making?

1. Inciting Investment in Debt

Not including investment losses in the tender lowers the minimum amount of debt that debtors have to repay through the system. Due to this, some might abuse personal rehabilitation to receive indemnification from excessive debt acquired from investment. If so banks, the creditors for personal rehabilitation, will suffer from losses. Accordingly, an employee of a commercial bank criticized that the new rule is unreasonable in an interview with Korea Economic Daily. Furthermore, investment in stocks or cryptocurrency is, strictly put, one’s personal choice. Thus, it is different from other reasons for rehabilitation, including business failures or struggles against a disease. Therefore, some criticize that it is irrational for the entire society to burden an individual’s loss gained from personal choice. Moreover, recently, the government enacted the Youth Special Debt Adjustment to commute interest formed by investment failure. However, many criticized that both the government and SLBC are paying off the personal debts of young people. Hence, the new rule of SLBC and the government’s program may lead to moral hazard issues. At the same time, the court is criticized for ostracizing those suffering from external hardships and focusing on those who invested solely for personal gain.

2. Loss Caused by Fluctuations in Value

Stocks and cryptocurrencies have more significant value volatility compared to other types of assets. If the value fluctuates after the permission of a repayment plan and settlement of the tender, both the creditor and debtor may experience loss. On July 5th, the SLBC official stated that the court would not raise the tender even though the value of the debtor’s assets increased after settling the liquidating value in an interview with Kukmin Ilbo. Even if the debtor may increase the value of their assets, the creditors will be paid according to the plan. In an interview with the SKT, a worker in his 50s said, “In common sense, it is fair to repay more if the value of stocks or cryptocurrencies rises,” thus, “it is unreasonable for the debtor to benefit in the process of repayment.” Furthermore, if the value of stock or cryptocurrency decreases after the contract, the debtor’s property will decrease at the moment of repayment compared to the moment of approving the plan. Thus, the debtor could have a lower tender minimum if he postpones the approval timing. These are serious problems, as stock and cryptocurrency have high-value volatility.

A Substantially Disadvantaged Creditor (news-journalonline.com)

Significance and Future of the New Rule

What the New Rule of the SLBC Signifies?

Personal rehabilitation limits the applier’s unsecured debt to under 1.5 billion won, and secured debt to under 1 billion won. Most of all, it is a system for faithful but unlucky debtors. Therefore, the new rule guarantees personal rehabilitation for honest debtors who can repay the tender steadily and have no excessive debt. In addition, as integrated payment companies such as Danal and The Boring Company have cryptocurrency as one of their payment methods, it is a natural sequence to reserve the cryptocurrency’s current state. The new rule, which only includes the asset’s current value, can benefit the debtor and creditor to accomplish a virtuous economic cycle. Lawyer Song Won-ho of law firm Solution insisted, “The new rule will allow for a more realistic repayment plan, and debtors will be able to return to society.” Meanwhile, Oh Se-hun, a team leader of Solution, said, “Though the new rule is for investment failures, there should be alternatives against abuse of the rule.”

Efforts for Virtuous Circulation of the Economy (economictimes.indiatimes.com)

Efforts for Overcoming the Concerns

There needs to be a balanced interpretation of the rule between the debtor and creditor: personal rehabilitation is for guaranteeing the rights of both stakeholders. Firstly, debtors should not abuse the system and try their best to repay their debt. Creditors must remember that personal rehabilitation benefits them more because they can get repaid a higher amount in the long run through personal rehabilitation rather than bankruptcy. Also, the SLBC should look out for over-interpreting the rule’s operation. Furthermore, penalties against “excessive waste, gambling, and other speculative activities” should be strictly applied to debtors. In addition, as the court enacted the rule, the court should try to resolve the misunderstanding that the nation and banks are repaying investment debt. As the SLBC explained the new rule in the Personal Bankruptcy System Seminar on July 1st and 2nd, the court should reduce resistance against running the new rule. For instance, the Financial Services Commission posted card news on its website and Instagram account on July 19th to resolve misunderstandings related to the Youth Special Debt Adjustment. As such, the SLBC can resolve misapprehension in the same way.

Nowadays, there are many people seeking ways to proliferate their property for various purposes. Therefore, stocks and cryptocurrencies with a comparatively highvalue volatility are becoming dangerous but attractive assets. Any cases of investment failure and economic breakdown will bear an economic recession for society. Personal rehabilitation is the solution to the problem and must settle as a steady system.

news_articles.title: 1.5kV GaN monolithic bidirectional switch on 8-inch silicon
news_articles.abstract: Researchers based mainly in China report the demonstration of an enhancement-mode high-voltage monolithic bidirectional switch (MBDS) developed on an 8-inch gallium nitride (GaN)-on-silicon (Si) platform using a method compatible with mainstream silicon electronics [Yingfei Sun et al, IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices, online 26 October 2026]. The team claims the first demonstration of a GaN BDS with a static breakdown voltage (BV) of more than 1.5kV on an 8-inch silicon substrate.
news_articles.content_html:
Researchers based mainly in China report the demonstration of an enhancement-mode high-voltage monolithic bidirectional switch (MBDS) developed on an 8-inch gallium nitride (GaN)-on-silicon (Si) platform using a method compatible with mainstream silicon electronics [Yingfei Sun et al, IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices, online 26 October 2026]. The team claims the first demonstration of a GaN BDS with a static breakdown voltage (BV) of more than 1.5kV on an 8-inch silicon substrate.

The MBDS process flow was gold-free with a view to enabling integration with low-cost mainstream silicon complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) transistor circuitry. Gold is widely used in GaN transistor manufacturing, but is poisonous to silicon CMOS performance. Enhancement (E)-mode devices (i.e. normally-off at 0V gate potential) are particularly favored in power applications due to reduced power consumption and to providing a safer situation in conditions of failure.

The team from University of Science and Technology of China, Suzhou Institute of Nano-Tech and Nano-Bionics and Xi’an Jiaotong–Liverpool University in China, University of Liverpool in the UK, and Guangdong Institute of Semiconductor Micro-Nano Manufacturing Technology in China, see their results as demonstrating “wafer-level manufacturability, bidirectional high-voltage potential, and basic switching functionality of the proposed 8-in GaN-on-Si MBDS platform.”

The researchers see potential for their MBDS deployment in high-efficiency power conversion as components of matrix converters, solid-state circuit breakers, T-type converters, bidirectional DC–DC converters, and battery management systems. By integrating the BDS in a monolithic format the device reduces the chip area and hence on-resistance power losses.

The epitaxial material for the MBDS (Figure 1) was grown by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition on 8-inch silicon: 5.1μm GaN buffer, 500nm GaN channel, 0.5nm aluminium nitride (AlN) spacer, 15nm Al0.15Ga0.85N barrier, and 80nm p-GaN gate.

Figure 1: p-GaN gate HEMT and the p-GaN gate MBDS on 8-inch CMOS-compatible architecture.

The gate was defined first in the transistor fabrication (Figure 2) to give a self-aligned structure. The gate process consisted of 100nm titanium nitride (TiN) deposited on the p-GaN and then patterned and etched. The TiN etch was achieved first with inductively-coupled plasma, and then a wet process to give a lateral undercut. The p-GaN was then plasma etched using a highly selective process recipe. The surface roughness after etching was 0.6nm, according to atomic force microscope (AFM) analysis.

Figure 2: Fabrication process flow, highlighting self-aligned gate-first process and AFM image of result.

The first interlayer dielectric (ILD1) passivation consisted of atomic layer deposition (ALD) AlN and 150nm plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) silicon dioxide (SiO2).

The team explains: “The ALD-AlN layer is used to mitigate surface-state-related trapping and leakage, whereas the PECVD-SiO2 layer provides the dielectric thickness required for subsequent field-plate integration.”

Separate devices were isolated from each other by nitrogen ion implants. Annealed ohmic metals were used for the transistor source and drain electrodes: Ti/Al/Ti/TiN.

A further 100nm PECVD SiO2 was used for ILD2, and 130nm for ILD3. Source (S)-connected field plates (FPs) were implemented: the lower FP1 consisting of TiN/Al/TiN, while the upper FP2 was TiN.

In the dual-gate MBDS the field plates were placed symmetrically: “This arrangement is referred to as the symmetric D-SFP configuration and is designed to provide staged electric-field modulation under both blocking polarities.”

The aim was to avoid the field peaking above critical and so not prematurely breaking down in the off-state.

Two metal (M1, M2) interconnection layers were enabled with intermetal dielectrics (IMDs), along with tungsten-plug (W-plug) and via processing.

The HEMT featured a 2μm gate (LG) separated from the source (LSG) and drain (LGD) by 2μm and 18μm, respectively. The threshold was 0.86V, giving normally-off/enhancement-mode operation. The on-resistance (RON) was 14.8Ω-mm. The gate leakage current was 30nA/mm at 6V. The off-state breakdown voltage (BV) was 1.5kV for 1μA/mm leakage. A device without FPs only managed 850V BV.

The ratio of dynamic/static RON was less than 1.3 for stressing up to 800V. The researchers say that this “is significantly better than reported values for conventional p-GaN gate HEMTs. This behavior is consistent with the combined electric-field management of the D-SFP configuration and the surface stabilization provided by the stacked passivation scheme, which reduce the peak electric field at the gate edge and suppress surface trapping, respectively, thereby mitigating electron injection under high-drain-bias OFF-state stress.”

Figure 3: (a) Equivalent circuit diagram and four-quadrant operation modes, p-GaN MBDS: (b) transfer characteristics with VG2S2 at 0V, (c) transfer characteristics with VG2S2 at 5V, (d) bidirectional output characteristics with VG2S2 at 0V, and (e) bidirectional output characteristics with VG2S2 at 5V.

The threshold for the MBDS was around 0.83V (Figure 3). The RON was near symmetric: 14.7Ω-mm and 14.9Ω-mm in the opposite flow directions. The device length was 25μm, including 3μm for the contact transfer length, so LS1S2 is 22μm. The calculated specific on-resistances (RON,SP) were 3.68mΩ-cm2 and 3.72mΩ-cm2.

The researchers also compare their work with that of other groups (Figure 4). The team comments: “The results indicate that the static BV of the present device is among the highest reported for GaN bidirectional switches fabricated on silicon substrates.”

Figure 4: (a) OFF-state bidirectional blocking characteristics and (b) benchmark of RON,SP versus static BV comparing GaN MBDSs on different substrates. Orange dashed line: theoretical limit for GaN monolithic bidirectional switches.

The group attributes the high static blocking performance to “the combined electric-field management of the D-SFP configuration and the surface stabilization provided by the ALD-AlN/PECVD-SiO2 passivation.”

The BV and RON,SP values result in a 0.61GW/cm2 Baliga figure of merit (BFOM, BV2/RON,SP). The researchers also tested the circuit under temperatures up to 150°C and 60Hz alternating current (AC) chopping behavior with up to 5kHz drive signal.

Tags: GaN monolithic bidirectional switch GaN 8-inch silicon ALD PECVD

The author Mike Cooke is a freelance technology journalist who has worked in the semiconductor and advanced technology sectors since 1997.

news_articles.title: SKKU Ranks 24th Globally in THE Interdisciplinary Science Rankings
news_articles.affiliations: 1. Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU), Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea

affiliations_data.text: Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU), Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea

news_articles.abstract: Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) ranked 24th globally and 1st among South Korean universities in the 2027 THE Interdisciplinary Science Rankings, released on November 18 by the UK-based higher education ranking agency Times Higher Education (THE). Out of 1,058 universities ranked worldwide, SKKU climbed 19 spots from 43rd place the previous year.
news_articles.content_html:
The THE Interdisciplinary Science Rankings evaluate universities' contributions and capabilities in interdisciplinary research that combines multiple academic fields. Universities are ranked based on 11 indicators across three pillars: research funding investment (inputs), institutional support for interdisciplinary research (process), and research outputs such as publications, citations, and reputation.

Behind this achievement is the university’s sustained commitment to convergence research centered on key fields such as energy and bio, following the establishment of the SKKU Institute for Convergence (SAINT) in 2013. SAINT and the SKKU Institute of Energy Science & Technology (SIEST)—home to the Department of Energy and the Department of Energy Science—serve as convergence research hubs where researchers across engineering, natural sciences, and AI collaborate. Within our department as well, faculty and students from diverse academic backgrounds—including physics, chemistry, materials science, and electronics—work together to tackle challenges in the energy and semiconductor sectors.

This year, the "Sungkyun Intelligent Energy Solution National Research Laboratory," bringing together 122 researchers across energy, semiconductors, AI, and power systems, was selected for the National Research Laboratory (NRL 2.0) project.

Moving forward, the Department of Energy and the Department of Energy Science plan to continue strengthening the university's interdisciplinary research competitiveness through convergence education and research that transcend traditional academic boundaries.

Source: S-PRESS, "SKKU Ranks 24th Globally in THE Interdisciplinary Science Rankings"

news_articles.keywords: Sodium bismuth titanate; Optical properties; DFT+U; Band structure
news_articles.abstract: This study explores how intrinsic interstitial defects can be used to modulate the electronic and optical properties of the Bi<sub>0.5</sub>Na<sub>0.5</sub>TiO<sub>3</sub> (BNT) (110) surface, a promising lead-free piezoelectric. We use first-principles calculations based on the DFT+U formalism, applying a Hubbard U of 10 eV to the Ti 3d states to ensure an accurate description of the correlated electronic structure. Our results show the pristine surface is a non-magnetic semiconductor, but the introduction of interstitials triggers a functional transformation. Na- and Bi-interstitials are shown to act as n-type dopants that create a metallic surface and induce a magnetic moment. In contrast, Ti- and O-interstitials introduce deep, localized states within the band gap but do not produce a net magnetic moment. Our finding also pointing out that interstitial defects create new pathways for optical absorption at energies below the pristine band gap, causing a significant redshift in the absorption edge. This work demonstrates that native point defects can serve as functional ways, allowing the BNT(110) surface to be tuned to a potential system with metallic, magnetic, or optical characteristics. These insights also offer a viable pathway for the rational design of complex oxide surfaces for next-generation electronic and optoelectronic devices.
news_articles.content_html:
1.INTRODUCTION

In recent years, the global imperative to develop environmentally friendly and sustainable technologies has intensified research into lead-free ferroelectric materials as high-performance alternatives to traditional systems (Zhang et al., 2021). A leading candidate in this field is Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3 (BNT), a complex perovskite that has attracted considerable attention for its excellent ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties, which rival those of the widely used but toxic Pb(Zr,Ti)O3 (PZT) (Wei et al., 2018). BNT is particularly appealing due to its non-toxic composition, a large remnant polarization of approximately 38 µC/cm2, and a high Curie temperature near 320°C (Zhang et al., 2021; Quan et al., 2014), which ensures stable performance across a broad range of operating temperatures. However, BNT also faces significant challenges, such as a high coercive field of around 73 kV/cm, which demands greater power for polarization switching and can limit device longevity (Zhang et al., 2021). The interest in BNT extends beyond its ferroelectric nature into the realm of multiferroics, materials where ferroelectricity coexists with magnetic ordering. Such materials are highly sought after for next-generation multifunctional devices, as they offer the transformative potential to control magnetic properties with electric fields and vice versa (Prinz et al., 1999). While true multiferroics are rare because the electronic requirements for ferroelectricity (typically empty d-orbitals) and ferromagnetism (partially filled d-orbitals) are often mutually exclusive, a growing body of work suggests that defect engineering can be used to induce magnetism in BNT (Prinz et al., 1999; Benedek et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2020). Recently, there have been numerous experimental and theoretical studies that have successfully linked room-temperature ferromagnetism in BNT to various intrinsic point defects, including Na+ or Ti4+ vacancies, oxygen vacancies, and general Na-deficiency (Lam et al., 2022; Dung et al., 2024).

A significant portion of the previous research on defect-induced magnetism in BNT has focused either on bulk properties or the (100) surface, which calculations often predict to be the most stable termination. However, a critical discrepancy exists between these theoretical models and experimental observations. In practice, the (110) orientation is consistently favored for the epitaxial growth of thin films and the faceting of single crystals, indicating that the (110) surface is more technologically and scientifically relevant for understanding the properties of real-world BNT materials (Pattanayak et al., 2019; Ruth et al., 2019; Ju et al., 2014). Therefore, our own recent work has provided initial first-principles evidence that complex surface defects on the BNT(110) surface are indeed capable of inducing magnetic moments (Lam et al., 2022; Dung et al., 2024). Despite these preliminary findings, a systematic and mechanistic investigation into the role of various self-defects on the BNT(110) surface remains a clear knowledge gap in the field. To fully claim the potential application, a detailed understanding of its electronic and optical properties under interstitial defects is essential.

This study aims to investigate the electronic and optical properties of BNT(110) by employing Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations with the Hubbard U correction (the DFT+U method) to rigorously investigate the influence of interstitial defects. This can lead to solutions of a underestimation of the band gap and an incorrect description of localized electronic and magnetic states. The DFT+U approach explicitly incorporates an on-site Coulomb interaction term to correct for this self-interaction error, enabling a more physically accurate depiction of the system. Using this advanced methodology, we will perform a comprehensive analysis of how intrinsic interstitial defects alter the atomic geometry, electronic band structure, and optical absorption spectra of the BNT(110) surface. Our goal is to provide a detailed, atomistic picture of defect-induced phenomena, offering valuable insights that can guide the rational design of lead-free ferroelectric materials for future high-performance and environmentally friendly electronic devices.

2.METHODS

All first-principles calculations were performed within the framework of Density Functional Theory as implemented in the CASTEP code (Clark et al., 2005). The electron exchange-correlation energy was described using the generalized gradient approximation with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof functional (Perdew et al., 1996). A plane-wave pseudopotential basis set was employed with a kinetic energy cutoff of 500 eV, and geometry optimizations were considered converged when the total energy difference was less than 1×10-6 eV/atom and the maximum Hellmann-Feynman force was below 0.01 eV/Å. The Brillouin zone was sampled using a 1×2×2 k-point mesh (Monkhorst et al., 1976). To provide a more accurate description of the localized Ti-3d electronic states, this standard DFT framework was augmented with an on-site Hubbard U correction, with U values of 10 eV applied. The BNT(110) surface investigated in this study was modeled using a periodic slab approach, constructed from the geometry-optimized primitive cell of rhombohedral BNT (R3c space group). The initial atomic positions were relaxed within the experimental cell volume, using lattice parameters of a = b = 5.488 Å and c = 13.504 Å, showing close agreement with experimental findings (Lü et al., 2014). A 3×2×1 supercell was then created by cleaving the primitive cell along the (110) plane, and a vacuum layer of 10 Å was added to prevent interactions between periodic layers.

3.RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

3.1.Electronic properties

Fig. 1 displays the optimized atomic structure of the pristine surface slab model from multiple viewpoints. The three-dimensional perspective in Fig. 1(a) illustrates the supercell used in the calculations, while the side view (Fig. 1(b)) and top-down view (Fig. 1(c)) reveal the specific atomic arrangement and surface termination. This structure was obtained after cleaving the geometry-optimized bulk rhombohedral (R3c) BNT crystal and allowing the atomic positions in the upper layers of the slab to fully relax. The top view in Fig. 1(c) shows an ordered and stable surface, characterized by the alternating arrangement of A-site cations (Na and Bi) and the network of corner-sharing TiO6 octahedra that form the basic perovskite structure. The side view in Fig. 1(b) reveals a slight surface rumpling, a common relaxation phenomenon where atoms in the outermost layer displace vertically to minimize surface energy.

Fig. 2 presents the electronic band structure and the projected density of states, calculated using the DFT+U method to accurately capture the effects of electron correlation. The calculated band structure, shown in Fig. 2(a), reveals that the pristine BNT(110) surface exhibits a p-type tendency characterized by the Fermi level lying closer to the valence band edge with a combined direct and indirect band gap of approximately 3.46 eV, with the valence band maximum at the Z point and the conduction band minimum at the G point of the Brillouin zone. This band gap value is significantly larger than those obtained from standard GGA calculations, a direct result of the Hubbard U correction applied to the Ti-3d orbitals, which rectify the well-known band gap underestimation issue of standard DFT. Further insight into the electronic structure is provided by the density of states plots in Fig. 2(b). The upper valence band, extending from approximately -5 eV to the Fermi level, is predominantly formed by O-2p orbitals, which show significant hybridization with Bi-6p and Ti-3d states, indicating strong covalent bonding. The bottom of the conduction band is mainly composed of unoccupied Ti-3d states, with a smaller contribution from Bi-6p states. Additionally, a deeper, isolated band around -9 eV is composed almost entirely of Bi-6s states, which are often linked to the stereochemically active lone pair of the Bi3+ cation. The symmetrical nature of the DOS and the absence of any states within the gap reaffirm that the pristine BNT(110) surface is non-magnetic, providing a crucial electronic reference for understanding the perturbations induced by the introduction of interstitial defects.

The spin-polarized density of states, shown in Fig. 3, further confirms electronic properties of pristine BNT(110). The perfect symmetry between the spin-up and spin-down components for the total DOS and for each constituent atom (Na, Bi, Ti, and O) is the definitive signature of a non-magnetic state. This indicates that for every electron in a spin-up state, there is a corresponding electron in a spin-down state at the same energy level, resulting in a total magnetic moment of zero.

Next, the introduction of interstitial defects profoundly alters the electronic band structure of the BNT(110) surface is illustrated in Fig. 4 (a)-(d). The presence of either a Na- or a Bi-interstitial, shown in Fig. 4 (a) and (b) respectively, induces a metallic character. Both Na and Bi atoms act as effective electron donors, shifting the Fermi level upwards from the top of the valence band into the conduction band, a clear signature of n-type doping. In these cases, the band gap of the host BNT(110) remains largely intact, but it becomes partially filled by the donated charge carriers. In contrast, the Ti- and O-interstitials, shown in Fig. 4 (c) and (d), introduce deep, relatively flat bands within the original band gap. These in-gap states are characteristic of localized electrons associated with the defect. For the Ti-interstitial, these defect states appear near the middle of the gap, while for the O-interstitial, they form closer to the valence band maximum. In addition, the Fermi level is pinned within these new states, drastically reducing the energy required for electronic excitation and fundamentally changing the conductive nature of the surface.

The spin-polarized density of states for each of the four interstitial defect configurations, presented in Figure 5, further confirms and clarifies the electronic and magnetic changes inferred from the band structures. For the Na- and Bi-interstitials, the Fermi level is shifted well into the conduction band, confirming the metallic, n-type character of the surface, and the asymmetric spin-up and spin-down components are definitive evidence that these defects are magnetic. The magnetic moment mainly contributed by Ti-3d orbital states. In contrast, the DOS for the Ti- and O-interstitials in Fig. 5(c) and (d) reveal a profound symmetry between the spin-up and spin-down states, confirming that these defects were not affect to ferromagnetic properties.

For comparison, Table 1 details quantitative data of the calculated magnetic moments, giving a precise measure of the effects seen in the spin-polarized density of states by integrating the net spin density. The data confirms that the pristine BNT(110) surface is non-magnetic with a total magnetic moment of zero. It shows that the Na- and Bi-interstitials induce small but non-zero magnetic moments of 0.11 μB and 0.13 μB, respectively, which arise from a small polarization distributed across all atom types, with the Ti atoms showing the largest partial moments. Conversely, the Ti-interstitial results in a negligible moment of 0.01 μB, and the O-interstitial produces a total moment of zero, indicating that these two defects are effectively non-magnetic.

To provide a real-space visualization of the induced magnetism and the resulting atomic arrangements, the spin density distributions and relaxed structures for the interstitial defects are shown in Fig. 6. First, Fig. 6 (a) and (b) illustrate the calculated spin density for the magnetically active Na- and Bi- interstitials, confirming that the induced magnetic moment is not confined to a single point but is distributed in the region surrounding the defect, with significant localization on the neighboring titanium and oxygen atoms of the host BNT(110). This spatial distribution is in excellent agreement with the spin-polarized density of states analysis, which identified the Ti-3d and O-2p orbitals as the primary origin of the magnetism. In contrast, Fig. 6 (c) and (d) show the final relaxed atomic geometries for the non-magnetic Ti- and O-interstitial defects. The absence of any spin density in these cases is consistent with the symmetric DOS plots observed previously, confirming their non-magnetic nature. While these defects do cause significant local lattice distortions to accommodate the extra atom, they do not lead to a net spin polarization of the BNT(110) surface. Thus, these spin densities provide a clear, qualitative distinction between the two classes of interstitial defects: those that magnetically polarize the surface and those that simply incorporate into the lattice without inducing a magnetic moment.

3.2.Optical properties

To understand how the electronic modifications induced by interstitial defects translate to the interaction under polarized light, we calculated the optical absorption properties of the pristine BNT(110) and BNT(110) with interstitial defects, as shown in Fig. 7(a)-(c). The optical absorption band gap was estimated using the Wood-Tauc method (Wood et al., 1972), which analyzes the absorption spectra according to the following relation:

(1)

where α is absorption coefficient, A is a constant, hν represents the photon energy (with h denoting Planck constant), and Eg is the optical band gap [17]. The exponent n depends on the type of electronic transition: n = 2 for direct allowed transitions, and n = 1/2 for indirect allowed transitions.

The absorption spectrum of the pristine surface, shown in Fig. 7(a), is characterized by a sharp absorption edge, consistent with its nature as a wide-band-gap in electronic band structure. Crucially, the electronic band structure calculation in Section 3.1 yielded an electronic band gap of approximately 3.46 eV. The corresponding Tauc plot analysis in Fig. 7(b) allows for the extrapolation of a direct optical band gap of approximately 3.3 eV. This close agreement between electronic band gap and optical band gap is a key finding, as it confirms that the fundamental optical absorption onset is primarily governed by the direct interband transition from the valence band maximum O-2p states) to the conduction band minimum (Ti-3d states), as is typical for clean, wide-band-gap perovskite oxides. The introduction of any of the four interstitial types leads to a notable redshift in the absorption edge and the appearance of significant absorption features at energies below the pristine band gap. This sub-gap absorption is particularly pronounced for the Ti- and O-interstitials, as clearly seen in the Tauc plots for indirect transitions in Fig. 7(c). These two defects introduce strong absorption tails that extend deep into the visible and near-infrared regions of the spectrum. This behavior is a direct optical signature of the localized in-gap states that were identified in the electronic structure analysis, as these states create new pathways for low-energy electronic transitions. While the Na- and Bi-interstitials also cause a redshift, their effect is less dramatic and is primarily associated with the metallic nature they induce. These results are fully consistent with the electronic structure results and demonstrate that defect engineering can be an effective strategy for tuning the optical response of BNT surfaces for potential optoelectronic applications.

Fig. 8 shows the calculated conductivity, dielectric function, refractive index, energy loss function, and reflectivity for the pristine BNT(110) in Fig. 8 (a), compared against the surfaces with Na-, Bi-, Ti-, and O-interstitials in Fig. (b)-(e), respectively. The following equations, as reported in Refs. (Luo et al., 2015; Naveed-Ul-Haq et al., 2021; Cappellini et al., 2000), are utilized to evaluate the interdependence among these properties:

Firstly, the optical conductivity describes the motion of charges in response to the light’s electric field. The real part represents the energy dissipated from the field. For the pristine surface, the real part is zero at low energies, confirming its insulating state. For the Na- and Bi-interstitial defects, the non-zero value of real parts at low energies are characteristic of metallic conduction. The Ti- and O-interstitial defects also show non-zero conductivity at low energies due to electronic excitations enabled by the in-gap states. Meanwhile, the imaginary part, which describes the inductive, out-of-phase response of the current, shows features that mirror the real part of the dielectric function, reflecting the relationship between polarization and conductivity.

Secondly, the imaginary part of the dielectric function ( ε2(ω)) , shown in the second row, directly represents optical absorption. For the pristine surface, absorption begins only above the band gap energy (~3.3 eV). In contrast, all interstitial defects introduce significant absorption at lower energies. The Ti- and O-interstitial defects show the most dramatic effect, exhibiting distinct new absorption peaks below 3 eV. These peaks are the direct optical response of electronic transitions involving the localized in-gap states. The Na- and Bi-interstitial defects produce a broader absorption tail at low energies, consistent with the metallic nature they induce. In contrast, the real part ( ε1(ω)) describes the material’s ability to store energy from an electric field. The value at zero energy represents the static dielectric constant, and the introduction of any interstitial defect keeps the static dielectric constant intact to the pristine surface.

Thirdly, the complex refractive index implies how light propagates through the material. The real part ( nω ) is the standard refractive index that determines the speed of light. The static refractive index is enhanced for all four defect cases compared to the pristine surface. This means light travels more slowly through the defective surfaces, a consequence of their increased polarizability. The imaginary part ( kω ), known as the extinction coefficient, is directly proportional to the absorption coefficient. Its spectrum closely follows that of ε2(ω)) , with the Ti- and O-interstitial defects showing prominent peaks at low energies corresponding to their strong sub-gap absorption.

The energy loss function describes the energy lost by fast electrons passing through the material. The primary double-peak in the loss spectrum, located from 8 eV to 15 eV for the pristine case, is associated with the plasma frequency, representing collective oscillations of valence electrons. The introduction of defects induced these peaks, leading to the flat and saturation of these peaks. As a result, energy loss in the interstitial structure was reduced.

Lastly, the reflectivity indicates the fraction of light reflected on the surface. Consistent with the energy-loss function spectra, the reflectivities are lower for all interstitial defect surfaces than for the pristine one. The entire reflectivity spectrum is modified by the defects, particularly in the low-energy region where the new absorption level alters the optical response.

4. ConclusionS

In this study, we have performed a comprehensive first-principles investigation using the DFT+U method to determine the impact of intrinsic interstitial defects on BNT(110) surface. Our calculations confirm that the pristine surface is a non-magnetic p-type semiconductor, but the introduction of interstitials fundamentally alters its character through two distinct pathways. Na- and Bi-interstitials act as n-type dopants, donating electrons to make the surface metallic and inducing a small but distinct magnetic moment of 0.11 to 0.13 μB. In contrast, Ti- and O-interstitials introduce localized, deep states within the original band gap but were found to be effectively non-magnetic behaviours. These findings demonstrate that intrinsic point defects are powerful tools for engineering the functionality of BNT surfaces. We also reported interstitial defects induced the complex optical properties, suggesting a viable strategy for tuning BNT for optoelectronic or photocatalytic applications.

dft_lectures.title: Lecture 1: Quantum Many-Body Problem, Hohenberg–Kohn Theorems & Kohn–Sham DFT
dft_lectures.subtitle: From the exact 3N-dimensional Schrödinger equation and Levy–Lieb constrained search to the self-consistent Kohn–Sham orbital formalism and Pulay/Kerker SCF mixing.
dft_lectures.author: Vu Tien Lam
dft_lectures.keywords: schrodinger born oppenheimer many-body hohenberg kohn levy lieb variational kohn-sham janak scf self-consistent field pulay kerker hartree density functional convergence
objectives: Explain why solving the interacting many-electron Schrödinger equation directly is exponentially intractable and derive the Born–Oppenheimer separation.
Master the Hohenberg–Kohn theorems and Levy–Lieb constrained search establishing electron density n(r) as the exact ground-state variable.
Derive the Kohn–Sham single-particle equations, Janak's theorem, and the physical distinction between KS eigenvalues and quasiparticle energies.
Trace the Self-Consistent Field (SCF) loop including Pulay DIIS density mixing and Kerker preconditioning against charge sloshing.
dft_lectures.contentHtml:
1.1 The Many-Body Problem & Born–Oppenheimer Approximation

Every equilibrium and dynamical property of a crystal, surface, or molecule—its lattice constants, electronic band gap, magnetism, optical spectrum, and catalytic activity—is governed by the non-relativistic time-independent many-body Schrödinger equation for N electrons at coordinates {ri} and M nuclei of charges ZI and masses MI at positions {RI}:

\hat{H}\,\Psi\!\left(\{\mathbf{r}_i\}, \{\mathbf{R}_I\}\right) = E\,\Psi\!\left(\{\mathbf{r}_i\}, \{\mathbf{R}_I\}\right)
(1.1)

In atomic units (ℏ = me = e = 4πε0 = 1, where lengths are in Bohr a0 = 0.529177 Å and energies in Hartree 1 Ha = 27.211386 eV), the exact molecular or crystalline Hamiltonian comprises five distinct physical operators:

\hat{H} = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_i^2 - \sum_{I=1}^{M}\frac{1}{2M_I}\nabla_I^2 - \sum_{i,I}\frac{Z_I}{\left|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{R}_I\right|} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{1}{\left|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j\right|} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{I\neq J}\frac{Z_I Z_J}{\left|\mathbf{R}_I - \mathbf{R}_J\right|}
(1.2)
Terms left to right: electronic kinetic energy Te, nuclear kinetic energy Tn, electron–nucleus Coulomb attraction Vne, electron–electron Coulomb repulsion Vee, and nucleus–nucleus Ewald repulsion EII.
📘 Definition — Born–Oppenheimer (Adiabatic) Approximation
Because nuclei are 1,836 to >400,000 times heavier than electrons (MI ≫ me), electrons relax almost instantaneously to any nuclear displacement. Factoring the wavefunction as Ψ({ri}, {RI}) ≈ ψel({ri}; {RI}) χnuc({RI}) decouples nuclear motion and solves the electronic problem at fixed nuclear positions {RI}. The parametric electronic ground-state energy plus EII defines the Potential Energy Surface (PES) E({RI}).

Under the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, the clamped nuclei produce a static external potential vext(r) = −∑I ZI / |r − RI|, reducing Eq. (1.2) to the interacting electronic Hamiltonian:

\hat{H}_{\mathrm{el}} = \hat{T}_{\mathrm{e}} + \hat{V}_{\mathrm{ee}} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}_i)
(1.3)

Why Wavefunction Methods Hit an Exponential Wall: Representing the antisymmetric wavefunction ψ(r1, …, rN) on a coarse 10-point 3D grid per electron requires 103N complex amplitudes. Even for a single Fe atom (N = 26), 1078 numbers exceeds the count of atoms in the observable universe. Density Functional Theory bypasses this exponential barrier completely.

1.2 Electron Density, Hohenberg–Kohn Theorems & Levy–Lieb Search

Instead of the 3N-dimensional wavefunction, DFT uses the 3-dimensional electron number density n(r)—a scalar physical observable depending on only three spatial coordinates (x, y, z):

n(\mathbf{r}) = N \int \mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}_2 \cdots \mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}_N \allowbreak\,\left|\psi(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N)\right|^2, \qquad \int n(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} = N
(1.4)
📘 Definition — Hohenberg–Kohn Theorem I (Uniqueness)
For any system of interacting electrons in a non-degenerate ground state, the ground-state density n0(r) uniquely determines the external potential vext(r) up to a trivial additive constant. Hence n0(r) uniquely determines the entire Hamiltonian, ψ0[n0], and every ground-state physical observable as a functional of n(r).
📘 Definition — Hohenberg–Kohn Theorem II (Variational Principle)
A universal functional FHK[n] independent of vext(r) exists such that E[n] = FHK[n] + ∫vext(r)n(r)d3r attains its exact global minimum E0 if and only if n(r) = n0(r): E[n] ≥ E[n0] = E0.

To eliminate the original v-representability restriction of Hohenberg and Kohn (1964) and cover degenerate ground states, Mel Levy (1979) and Elliott Lieb (1983) formulated the rigorous Constrained-Search Functional minimizing over all antisymmetric N-electron wavefunctions yielding a given density n(r):

F_{\mathrm{LL}}[n] = \min_{\psi \to n}\langle \psi | \hat{T}_{\mathrm{e}} + \hat{V}_{\mathrm{ee}} | \psi \rangle, \qquad E_0 = \min_{n}\left\{\, F_{\mathrm{LL}}[n] + \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,n(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} \,\right\}
(1.5)

1.3 The Kohn–Sham Ansatz (1965) & Janak's Theorem

Although FLL[n] is formally exact, direct density-only kinetic energy functionals (such as Thomas–Fermi) fail to reproduce atomic shell structure or chemical bonding. Walter Kohn and Lu Jeu Sham solved this by mapping the interacting system onto a fictitious system of N non-interacting electrons moving in an effective local potential veff(r) whose ground-state density equals the exact interacting density:

n(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i\,\left|\phi_i(\mathbf{r})\right|^2
(1.6)
where φi(r) are orthonormal Kohn–Sham orbitals and fi ∈ [0, 2] (or [0, 1] per spin channel) are occupation numbers.

The Kohn–Sham total energy functional separates four explicitly computable pieces from a single remaining unknown term, the exchange–correlation functional Exc[n]:

E_{\mathrm{KS}}[n] = T_{\mathrm{s}}\!\left[\{\phi_i\}\right] + \int v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})\,n(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} + E_{\mathrm{H}}[n] + E_{\mathrm{xc}}[n] + E_{\mathrm{II}}
(1.7)
T_{\mathrm{s}}\!\left[\{\phi_i\}\right] = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i \int \phi_i^*(\mathbf{r})\,\nabla^2\phi_i(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{H}}[n] = \frac{1}{2}\iint \frac{n(\mathbf{r})\,n(\mathbf{r}')}{\left|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'\right|}\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}'
(1.8)

Imposing stationarity δEKS / δφi* = 0 with Lagrange multipliers ϵi enforcing orthonormality ⟨φi|φj⟩ = δij yields the Kohn–Sham single-particle equations:

\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_0}\nabla^2 + v_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r})\right]\phi_i(\mathbf{r}) = \varepsilon_i\,\phi_i(\mathbf{r}), \qquad v_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r}) = v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}) + v_{\mathrm{H}}(\mathbf{r}) + \frac{\delta E_{\mathrm{xc}}[n]}{\delta n(\mathbf{r})}
(1.9)
💡 Physical Insight — Physical Meaning of Kohn–Sham Eigenvalues & Janak's Theorem
Strictly speaking, Kohn–Sham eigenvalues ϵi are Lagrange multipliers of the auxiliary non-interacting system, not exact single-electron removal energies. However, Janak's Theorem proves ∂EKS/∂fi = ϵi, and for the exact functional the highest occupied eigenvalue equals the negative exact ionization potential (ϵHOMO = −I). In practice, KS eigenvalues provide an excellent starting description of band dispersion and orbital ordering, while quantitative band gaps require Hybrid DFT (HSE06) or many-body GW corrections (Lecture 2).

1.4 The Self-Consistent Field (SCF) Loop, Pulay Mixing & Kerker Damping

Because vH[n] and vxc[n] depend on the output density nout(r), Eq. (1.9) must be iterated to self-consistency. Simple linear mixing diverges in metallic slabs because the Hartree potential scales as 4π/q2 at long wavelengths (q → 0), causing charge sloshing. Modern codes (CASTEP, VASP) combine Pulay DIIS with Kerker reciprocal-space preconditioning:

G_{\mathrm{Kerker}}(q) = A\,\frac{q^2}{q^2 + q_0^2}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{in}}^{(k+1)}(\mathbf{q}) = n_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(k)}(\mathbf{q}) + G_{\mathrm{Kerker}}(q)\,R_{\mathrm{opt}}^{(k)}(\mathbf{q})
(1.10)
Kerker preconditioning damps long-wavelength q → 0 charge sloshing while accelerating short-wavelength convergence (controlled in CASTEP via mix_charge_amp and mix_charge_gmax).

n(r)Ground-state valence electron number densitye / Å3 (or e / Bohr3)
φi(r), ϵiKohn–Sham auxiliary orbitals & eigenvaluesÅ−3/2, eV (or Hartree)
EH[n]Classical electron–electron Coulomb (Hartree) repulsion energyeV
Exc[n]Exchange–correlation energy (Pauli + correlation + kinetic diff.)eV

HANDS-ON PRACTICE IN DATA ANALYSIS
🧪 Inspect Live SCF Convergence & Kohn–Sham Logs
  1. In Data Analysis → ⚡ Conv., select any CASTEP job (for example, J1+4 CASTEP Energy or KCoHCF+K).
  2. Observe the Total Energy / Enthalpy vs. Iteration curve relaxing smoothly toward the variational minimum E0, and the log10(ΔE / atom) curve crossing the green dashed elec_energy_tol threshold.
  3. Switch to 📝 Files → .castep to inspect the exact SCF loop table (Total Energy, Fermi Energy, Energy gain per atom) and .param to tune elec_energy_tol, mix_charge_amp, and max_scf_cycles.
